terms.gloss: voluntary, done of one’s own will
evidence: Cic. Off. 1.28: sī est voluntārium (Lewis & Short)
Caes. B.C. 3.91, of soldiers: volunteers (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Of people, willing, serving of their own accord; as a noun, voluntāriī m. pl. are volunteers (Caes., Liv.). Of things, done or chosen freely: discessus voluntārius, a departure of one’s own choosing (Cic. Att. 9.13.4).

terms.gloss: voluntarily, of my (your, his) own accord
terms.grammar: phrase: ablative, in good prose always with the possessive
evidence: Cic. Fam. 9.14.2: tuō jūdiciō et tuā sponte facere (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The everyday way to say that someone did a thing without being made to.

evidence: Cic. Leg. 1.48: līberālitās grātuītane est an mercēnāria? (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: For voluntary work in the sense of unpaid: done without pay or reward.

phrases.latin: Hoc patrium est, potius cōnsuēfacere fīlium suā sponte rēctē facere quam aliēnō metū.
phrases.english: That is a father’s way: to get his son used to doing right of his own accord, rather than from fear of someone else.

phrases.latin: movērī vetuisse puerum dōnec suā sponte experrēctus esset
phrases.english: she forbade anyone to move the boy until he had woken up of his own accord

sources: Lewis & Short: voluntarius · Lewis & Short: sponte · Lewis & Short: gratuitus
